title: Enrollment Growth Spurred by Commitment to Applied Learning for Students
text: Enrollment Growth Spurred by Commitment to Applied Learning for Students - It’s been ten years since Wichita State closed what had been Braeburn Golf Course, hurling the university and Wichita community on a bold new path forward. Many of us – back in 2014 – wondered with trepidation and excitement what was ahead for Shocker Nation by venturing into a new concept called Innovation Campus. After lots of hard work – which included tension and difficult decisions – and strategic planning plus some good luck, our university has been forever changed. While the Innovation Campus represents physical change and hundreds of millions of dollars in investments in more than 20 new structures on campus, the Innovation Campus’ potentially greatest impact has resulted in record-crushing enrollment for the second year in a row. For all the students and families out there embarking on a college search, this is the perfect moment to take notice of a Yellow and Black star on the rise. Last week Wichita State announced our largest enrollment ever in the university’s 129-year history at 17,700 students. A few highlights of note that the Office of Admissions is proud of as it relates to Future Shockers: Fall 2024, Fall 2023, Fall 2022 and Fall 2021 represent the four largest freshmen classes in the university’s history. For the fourth year in a row, total new degree-bound undergraduate freshmen and transfer students increased. This consistency in year-over-year growth is unrivaled in the state of Kansas. With another boost in transfer students, Wichita State can make the claim of being Kansas’ #1 transfer destination for 13 years running. Enrollment of new out-of-state students continues to rise as more students are making the trek to the largest city in Kansas to be a part of Shocker Nation. You’re wondering what’s the why? How has Wichita State bucked a downward trend of overall higher education enrollment in the Midwest? I bring you back to our now ten-year-old Innovation Campus and the university’s ultra-fine focus on applied learning for every student regardless of their major. We’ve baked applied learning experiences into every single undergraduate degree program because we think it’s just that important for Shockers to stand tall in the crowd of college graduates. When our grads sit down to interview for their first job out of college or for law or medical school acceptance, we know our students will demonstrate they’ve not only completed the required traditional academic courses, but also that they’ve applied their classroom education in the real world through an internship, a clinical rotation, a research opportunity, or other experience in the field. Our Innovation Campus has brought dozens of business and community partners to campus where – in exchange for them to have space – they have to hire our students for internships. Our students are literally going from their classroom to their internship, all within the confines of our 330-acre campus. As one example, I recently had lunch on campus with an executive at a Fortune 600 company, NetApp, which has a major presence on our campus. He informed me they have more than 50 of our students working for them on a multitude of projects. Here are four recent stories of Shockers’ summer 2024 internship experiences to demonstrate this point further and how these applied learning experiences stretch on- and off-campus: Nataleigh Holguin | Marketing | Internship at Hasbro Rafael Guereque | Forensic Science | Internship with Wichita Police Department Lauren Coffman | Biomedical Engineering | Internship at NASA Ashlynn Riggs | Education | Teacher Apprentice at the Wichita State Child Development Center I’ll end with one last glimpse into why we think Wichita State has grown so much in the last ten years. Recently our president, Dr. Rick Muma, asked me to join him on his Forward Together pod/videocast to talk more about the university’s efforts in applied learning. Between our relentless focus on applied learning and our development of the Innovation Campus, it’s been the enrollment game changer for our flourishing university. My hope is that you’ll choose to see this all for yourself through a campus visit – either in-person or virtually . With an Innovation Campus reaching a decade milestone, our enrollment trending up and more applied learning experiences from companies and organizations coming our way each day, I can’t tell you enough how exciting it is to be a part of a university that is ascending to our greatest heights yet. title: Out-of-State-Shockers: Sophie Walter
text: Out-of-State-Shockers: Sophie Walter - Student Ambassadors Brailey Lanning, Cary Doerflinger, Sophie Walter and Josef Schuller at Discover Wichita State: Oklahoma City. The most common question I get on panels or tours is, “You're from Wisconsin. Why are you going to school in Wichita, Kansas?” To be fully honest, it is a very long story and journey. It all started in the fifth grade when one of my extended cousins was getting married in Wichita and my grandma wanted to take me to see her sister and family for the first time since 2012. Five of my cousins who live here all graduated from Wichita State. Ever since that wedding in November of 2015, my grandma and I kept coming back to visit my family here. My family here would dress me up in Wichita State gear as a joke and I slowly started to love the city and the school. Photo courtesy of Sophie Walter I started looking at colleges the summer before my junior year of high school and I wasn’t fully sold on moving far away from home, but it was still on my radar. My grandma took me to Wichita for my 16th birthday and on my actual birthday, I toured Wichita State. I immediately fell in love with the school, and I remember calling my mom back in Wisconsin and saying this is the school I see myself at and I want to go to. She was happy for me but wanted me to keep my options open, so I did. However, Wichita State checked all my boxes, like having your bedroom with laundry in your dorm room and all the security measures to make sure students feel safe. Photo courtesy of Sophie Walter Sophie and her roommates at Wichita State. Another big thing I was looking for in college was a good study abroad program. Wichita State has a great deal of partnerships with universities all over the world and with some of them, I can pay WSU tuition to live abroad. For me, that was a huge deal. I’m a business student so all the opportunities that are provided through the Barton School of Business were also a huge selling point for me because I could get an internship in the field I was interested in before graduating college. Even if you are not a business student, there are many opportunities for students to get jobs and internships so they can get experience in the field they are interested in before graduation. In November of my senior year, I came to Wichita State to compete in the Distinguished Scholarship Invitational, which awards three $64,000 scholarships. Even though I didn’t win, this competition was the final push I needed to go to Wichita State. I met so many fellow students, professors, mentors and one of my future roommates/best friends. So, I encourage people to apply to DSI if they can because it is such a meaningful experience. One of the major things I got out of DSI was being nominated for the Student Ambassador Society. I didn’t know this at the time, but it was one of the best things that came out of this experience. Sophie and Kyra Bergman writing postcards for SAS. Once arriving at Wichita State I felt nervousness and excitement, but slowly that started to fade because even though I was over 12 hours from my family and everything I had ever known, and I was ready to get started. I joined the Student Ambassador Society (SAS) and since then have so many amazing people. Some of my closest friends are in that organization. I get to talk to prospective students about my experience and through that I have felt less alone. Joining SAS is the best choice I have made here because I meet so many people who help me realize I have a place here and want to stay. Also, it opens doors for me like working as a Shocker Navigator and as a student assistant in Admissions. So, my biggest piece of advice is to get involved whether it's with an organization, Greek life, or an on-campus job because you will meet the best people and find your home. I truly believe coming to Wichita State from Wisconsin was the best decision possible for me and I can’t imagine being anywhere else. title: Five Ways To Adjust to Campus Life After Transferring
text: Five Ways To Adjust to Campus Life After Transferring - Matt Crow/Undergraduate Admissions Transferring from Garden City Community College to Wichita State University was a major change for me. The idea of going from a small town in southwest Kansas to the largest city in the state was terrifying. Thankfully, adjusting to my new lifestyle has been easier than I imagined. Here are five tips that helped me adjust quickly! Sign up for a mentorship program/ success coaching Mentorship programs allow you to get advice from someone who has been on campus for a while. You can ask them all the questions you have and they will help you get an idea as to what to expect. I signed up for the ACE Mentoring Program which is a mentoring program for incoming engineering students. I was able to meet someone who was studying the same major as I was and who had similar interests. Additionally, each program has a success coach. Their role is to help students develop essential skills that will assist their academic careers. Find a group or organization that catches your interest It’s scary not knowing anyone in a new environment, so why not try to meet new people who have similar interests as you ? I had a friend who invited me to a HALO (Hispanic American Leadership Organization) event in my first semester on campus . I went and I made new friends! They made the transition less scary since they already had time on campus. Attend some events on or off campus There can be quite a bit going on in Wichita. Go to one of the many events the city has to offer whether it be watching a FREE Shocker basketball game or attending Open Streets ICT. There are so many things to experience. Do community service No better way to learn about the community than by helping the community! Wu’s Big Event is Wichita State's largest day of volunteering. It is a great chance to meet other students and members of the community as you all do your part in giving back. The Community Service Board is the place to go for more information on volunteering opportunities. Try to spend as much time on campus as you can Whether it be in the Rhatigan Student Center, Shocker Success Center or Woolsey Hall, being on campus gives you an opportunity to socialize and meet new people. Plus, by exploring campus, you get to learn more about the things Wichita State has to offer! Blog home All posts Yovani Cruz Yovani is a mechanical engineering major from Garden City, Kansas. He works for the Office of Admissions as a Transfer Guide after transferring from Garden City Community College. title: First-Gen to Director: Tales and Tips for First-Gen College Students
text: First-Gen to Director: Tales and Tips for First-Gen College Students - I don’t know what people see or think when they first meet me on campus, but I’d be willing to bet what they don’t see: a first-generation college student. That’s okay. We’re rather hard to spot. We don’t carry ourselves a certain way; we don’t talk a certain way; we don’t dress differently; there’s no neon sign hovering above us with an arrow. At least, I’m not aware of any of these things. I grew up in Pennsylvania, the product of a hard-working, blue-collar family. There were the shadows of Allentown’s factories and the ever-glowing smokestacks of Bethlehem Steel. My father, who was a machinist, dreamed of something more for me and my younger brother, as most parents do. He and my mother wanted something a little bit more for our futures. But what was that? Money was first and foremost a worry, and he and my mother knew what the answer probably was: an education. Better yet, a college education. I could taste the idea of college before I even knew, really, what college was or meant. Everyone knew one thing about me, though, and that was I was the family bookworm, the book nerd. On a summer visit not too long ago, my mother asked me, “Kerry. Do you ever go anywhere without a book? Do you ever just stop reading?” I looked at her with a combination of bewilderment and horror. No. Of course not. That’s unthinkable. Even now. Even though I was in what was known as the “college prep” track in high school, college didn’t become a true reality until perhaps my sophomore year. Student loans would definitely become part of my life, for a very long time indeed, but once I knew I could actually get to college, oh. The joy of just the thought! I met with plenty of college representatives who came to my high school throughout my junior year, took my SATs, filled out college applications to every school I thought was reasonable – and all but one was to a state college in Pennsylvania – and kept my fingers crossed. There were two that appealed to me, but I had my sights set on one in particular: Mansfield University. MU (my father enjoyed calling it “Moo You” because of its rural location) appealed to me because it was small, and just the right distance from home: close to four hours away. When I received my acceptance letter, I was thrilled. Finally! I was going to college. It wasn’t a dream anymore. But then...a little fear and trepidation set in. Who was I? Who did I think I was? No one, absolutely no one, in my family had ever gone to college. I realized that in so many ways I’d be on my own, navigating waters no one could help me with. And I have to be perfectly honest here. What was my biggest fear? I was afraid I would fail. I think these days we call it something like “imposter syndrome.” If that’s the case, I had a good dose of it, and certainly not without reason. Once again, no one in my family had ever been to college, and not because they weren’t smart enough. They had never had the opportunity I now had. I didn’t want to let myself down, of course, but I didn’t want to let my father and mother down. Regardless of those fears, off I went in August of 1990 (please don’t do any math.) Before I did so, I bought a little book called How to Succeed in College, or something like that. I highlighted and annotated the heck out of that thing throughout the summer of 1990. I scrutinized it. Then I kept my fingers crossed and did the only thing I could do, and that was my best. How well do I remember that first semester of college? Very well indeed. My first day of class was Monday, August 25. I had a sweet schedule that semester! My first class was at noon on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, and that was Introduction to Art. From there I went to Introduction to Politics, and then I had Literature of the Western World I, and from there... Yes. That first semester was definitely memorable. Remember: I was scared. When you’re afraid, you remember. At orientation, I don’t recall a whole lot being said about time management or tips about studying. Maybe that came up, but in the end, it was just me, and a lot of new territory. Okay. Now you can do some math. All that happened a long, long time ago. But in the end, there is a happy ending. Or maybe there isn’t an ending at all. Not only did I do well, I kept on going! These days, my younger brother likes to joke, “Kerry went off to college and never really came home.” All joking aside, he’s right. I didn’t. I found “my home,” and I found “my people.” I’m at home being a fiction writer (yes – I not only teach stories to students, I write them) and working in academia, and what I love more than teaching literature and other courses is working with students and getting to know them. All my students have unique lives and stories to tell, and definitely a different course in life than I may have taken. I will say, that as a Writing Center Director and someone who works with a lot of first-generation students, and as a former Orientation Fellow, I am often asked how to be successful in college. Unfortunately, there’s no blueprint or step-by-step guarantee for success – however you define success – but I do have some tips to try. That’s what I say to fellow creative writers. I never say, “Do this.” Instead, taking a cue from a writer named Natalie Goldberg (author of Writing Down the Bones and Wild Mind. Living The Creative Life) I say, “Try this.” It’s only two words, so don’t be scared. Just “try this”: 1. Accept that you belong. I think this happens to a lot of first-year college students, not just first-generation. But you didn’t get to college magically. You worked hard. You belong in college. It wasn’t an accident! 2. Take your classes seriously, even if you think they don’t apply to your major. Remember that Introduction to Art class I mentioned? I wasn’t an Art major, and I didn’t get the Introduction to Theater class I wanted to be in. However, I still remember a lot of what I learned in that class, and as someone who loves art and museums, it’s nice to see some things on a new level. Oh! And I discovered, as a writer, how art can inspire art. 3. Try not to overwhelm yourself with extracurricular activities. Get involved! It’s nice to be involved. Just don’t get so involved that you lose sight of why you’re really in college and lose track of the real priorities. Ease yourself into a routine you can actually manage. 4. Believe in yourself. It’s great to hear nice things from other people (friends, parents, professors, significant others), but you have to believe in yourself, too. 5. Breathe. This is a hard one. But on days when things get tough and overwhelming, doing something simple for yourself–just you–can mean the world, and take away some of the stress. 6. Get to know your professors. We don’t bite! And we can help you navigate. I’m in touch with so many of my professors who helped along the way. Office hours are fantastic things, and I wish more students took advantage of them. Office hours are for students. Some of my colleagues even have “coffee hours” and meet their students at Starbucks on campus. 7. Take advantage of academic assistance. It’s free, and such services are there to help you. At Wichita State, you’ll find a lot of those services – the Writing Center, Math Lab, Physics Help and Supplemental Instruction – in the new Shocker Success Center . Don’t confuse these services with this kind of thinking: “Oh, if I need help I’m doing something wrong. I’m not a good student." Far from it! We all need a boost once in a while, or some clarification, or even just another set of eyes. As a writer myself...I know even the “best” writers out there have editors. If you’ve heard of F. Scott Fitzgerald, you might want to Google “Maxwell Perkins.” 8. Breathe some more. See No. 5. 9. Did you stumble? Get a grade you didn’t like? Dust yourself off and get back up. Ask yourself some questions: Could I have done something differently? Did I try my best? Did I give myself enough time? Did I put enough effort into a project? Do I need to meet with my professor? Take some control and some responsibility. 10. Look around for opportunities. You’ll see lots of posters and advertisements for things across campus. If something intrigues you, explore it! That’s how doors can open up. Contact Kerry Jones at kerry.jones@wichita.edu . Connect with us Wichita State Admissions wichitastateadmissions wheatweet wichitastateu Future Shocker shockerexp
reason: Provides useful tips and advice for first-generation college students

title: The Cohen Honors College; Growth, Learning and Free Coffee
text: The Cohen Honors College; Growth, Learning and Free Coffee - Photo courtesy of Tania Molina Tania Molina during the Cohen Honors College's Lead for Tomorrow program. As a first-year student at Wichita State, my number one goal was to get involved and learn about the campus and the community. I learned about the Dorothy and Bill Cohen Honors College during my first-year orientation and through being involved in the National Honors Society in high school. Worried about how strenuous it could be to maintain the GPA and curricular requirements, my immediate thought was, “I don’t want to put that type of pressure on myself again for four more years.” So, I did not apply. As the semester went on, I heard more and more about the Honors College, and that free coffee and unlimited free printing kept luring me in, so I decided to apply for the benefits. As I learned more and more about it, I regretted not applying sooner. The Honors College has allowed me to grow academically and personally. They strongly believe in directly applying what they teach and offer many courses that exemplify this. From traveling to the Grand Canyon every winter to Paraguay in the summer, Honors supports you. I had the opportunity to participate in Lead for Tomorrow, a research and design thinking course that connected us to the Wichita Habitat for Humanity. It presented challenges for our team and tested our creativity and grit, but the best part of this course was traveling and learning hands on! Discovering and learning about Memphis, Tennessee, with my cohort motivated me for the work we were doing. As an Honors student, you’re doing incredible things as a student and the skills learned and applied will last you a lifetime. Photo courtesy of Tania Molina I’ve also participated in their Paraguay Honors Service-Learning program, and it was completely covered by a scholarship available to Honors students only: The Cohen Enhancement Scholarship . In Paraguay, I also did some research on healthcare accessibility and affordability, as well as the measures and regulations the country takes to implement and ensure each citizen is receiving adequate healthcare. Being both passionate about healthcare affordability and my Latina heritage, the Paraguay course enriched me even more in ways I never thought possible. Photo courtesy of Tania Molina There are so many ways to get involved in the Honors College, be it through coursework or with other activities and events they hold, like monthly colloquiums with the first-year students, or being a part of the Honors Student Council or an Honors Ambassador. You are destined to meet intellectual people who are learning what meaningful work means to them, and actively applying it in their communities and on campus, making them a truly distinguished Honors student. If you were hesitant about the Honors curriculum and the overall experience as an Honors student, I hope my experience can help you decide if the Honors College is a good fit for you. If you have more questions, don’t hesitate to reach out to the amazing staff members in the Honors office. I hope to see you around the honors student lounge soon for some free coffee and printing, and I hope you'll be ready to make an impact on the world! title: Things To Know When Filling Out the 2025–26 FAFSA Form
text: Things To Know When Filling Out the 2025–26 FAFSA Form - Wichita State Strategic Communications "It’s that time – FAFSA app is here! Everybody knows there is not a better time of year. Hear that sound, money has been found. Hip-hip-hooray! It’s FAFSA Completion!” (Sung to the tune of “ Christmas Vacation ”, adapted by Amanda Duffy) The 2025-2026 FAFSA form is now available for all students and their contributors (i.e. parent or spouse). Wichita State University’s priority date to submit your 2025-2026 Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) is April 1, 2025 . Don’t miss out on this opportunity to secure your financial aid for the upcoming academic year, especially need-based aid! Here are some frequently asked questions regarding the 2025-2026 FAFSA. Q: How long does it take to complete the FAFSA? A: It should take less than one hour to complete the FAFSA form. Q: What do I need to get my application completed? A: 1) FSA ID & Password – this can take up to three days for Federal Student Aid to verify your Social Security Number and until it has been verified, you cannot access the FAFSA. 2) You and your contributor’s Social Security Numbers 3) You and your contributor’s 2023 federal tax returns 4) Records of child support received 5) Balances of cash/savings/checking account(s) 6) Net worth of investments, businesses and farms Q: I support myself. Why do I have to include my parent’s information on the FAFSA? A: Even if you support yourself, live on your own or file your own taxes, you may still be considered a dependent student for FAFSA purposes. The FAFSA form asks a series of questions to determine dependency status. If you’re independent, you won’t need to include your parents’ information on your FAFSA form. But if you are dependent, you must provide your parents’ information. Q: How long does it take for Federal Student Aid to send a contributor their invitation email? A: A contributor should typically receive an email notification to complete their portion of the form within 1-3 days of the student submitting their application. Q: What is Wichita State University’s Federal School Code? A: 001950 Q: What happens after I submit my application? A: Once you click ‘Submit’, Federal Student Aid will process your information and generate a FAFSA Submission Summary which details your estimated financial aid eligibility, including your Student Aid Index (SAI), and send this information to colleges you listed on your application. Then, colleges use this data to create their individual financial aid packages based on your eligibility and their available funds. However, sometimes the colleges may need more information from you before creating the financial aid packages. If this is the case, the Office of Financial Aid & Scholarships will reach out to students through their Shocker Email. Once we receive all the needed information then we will be able to send an offer on your financial aid package. Q: When will Wichita State University receive my FAFSA application? A: We will receive your FAFSA within two business days of you submitting your application to Federal Student Aid. Q: My parents make too much money, so I won’t qualify for any aid. Why should I fill out the FAFSA? A: Don’t make assumptions about what you’ll get – fill out the application and find out. By completing the form, you are applying for federal and state grants, work-study and loans – not to mention the institutional aid that you could qualify for with the results of your federal aid application. And the best part – it’s FREE! Q: What if my financial situation has changed since filing the FAFSA? A: You should contact the Office of Financial Aid & Scholarships at Wichita State University to discuss the change in your financial situation. You may need to provide documentation to support your change in financial situation. We are located in Jardine Hall, Room 203 and can be contacted at 316-978-3430. Our office is open from 8 a.m. - 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. (Note: The university will be closed from the end of business day Friday, Dec. 20, 2024, and will reopen on Monday, Jan. 6, 2025). Q: I didn’t receive enough money for college. Am I just out of luck? A: You still have options! If you received federal, state and institutional aid but still find yourself having to fill the gap between what your financial aid cover and what you owe the college, consider scholarships through ScholarshipUniverse , part-time work, and Wichita State University’s payment plan through Accounts Receivable . We are here to help unlock every dollar possible at Wichita State University! The 2025-2026 FAFSA is available at studentaid.gov . If you experience any issues while attempting to complete your application, you can access Federal Student Aid’s Help Center 24/7/365. You can call them at 1-800-433-3243, live chat with Aiden the Owl or send an email. We are committed to helping you in any way we can with your 2025-2026 application or any other financial aid concern you may have. You can call, chat, or schedule a financial aid appointment with one of our amazing advisors! Want to talk? Our phone number is (316) 978-3430 or (855) 978-1787. Want to type? Chat with us ! Want to schedule an appointment? You can select the appropriate advisor through WSU’s Navigate system – just use your myWSU ID and password to log into Navigate. We can meet in-person, over the phone or even virtual! Stay up to date with our events and on social media @wichitastatefinaid . Outside of visiting us with questions one-on-one, we offer workshops to help with FAFSA completion. We are here to invest in you! Reach out to her office for questions about the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA)! title: Scholarship Extension Now Available for New Incoming Freshmen
text: Scholarship Extension Now Available for New Incoming Freshmen - Matt Crow/Undergraduate Admissions Wichita State fans at a men's basketball game in Charles Koch Arena. With just a handful of months left of high school, seniors and their parents may feel like time is flying by fast. Before you know it, prom season, senior skip day and graduation will be on your doorstep. For seniors who feel like their window to apply for college may be closing, Wichita State has a jolt of good news coming your way. We’re thrilled to announce Wichita State University has adjusted the deadline for freshmen scholarship consideration to March 1, 2025 for high school seniors. For students who haven’t yet applied, dedicating just 10-15 minutes to complete our admission application and paying the application fee means they’ll be automatically considered for Wichita State’s largest comprehensive scholarship program. Check out our scholarship grid below and odds are good you’ll find a scholarship you qualify for based on GPA only, or potentially a higher scholarship based on a combination of your GPA and ACT/SAT. If you qualify, our Financial Aid team will soon have an official award letter on its way to you after you’ve applied for admission! No strings attached and it gives you plenty of time to decide by May 1, 2025 – the national college decision day – whether or not wearing black and yellow is destined to be part of your college future. Wichita State University's Freshman Scholarship chart: Amounts for Kansas residents and students from surrounding states who are eligible for tuition discounts are un-bolded. Amounts for out-of-state residents who are not eligible to receive tuition discounts based on their residency are in bold. The scholarship amount shown is the total over four years. More details are available via the Freshmen Scholarship page . While our university has seen recent extraordinary growth – including the four largest freshmen classes in the university’s 129-year history occurring in the last four years in a row – we’re excited to give even more students the opportunity to join Shocker Nation and give them a start with a four-year scholarship offer. Our niche is helping students pursue their academic goals and chase their professional dreams through applied learning experiences. Last year Shockers had more than 9,000 internships and on-campus positions, earning more than $30 million in wages. If you’ve held off on applying for college because you’re not sure if you want to start your career first, we can help you do both by assisting with college funding along the way through the combined power of scholarships and paid applied learning. We’ve included the scholarship grid above that applies to Kansas residents and the thousands of students from eight surrounding states who benefit from heavily discounted tuition rates. Trust me! Spending 15 minutes to complete the application could deliver you as much as a $16,000 scholarship. For the full scholarship amounts and details – including out-of-state scholarships for students who can’t tap tuition discounts – visit our scholarship site . Your senior year will melt away quickly, but we’ve got you covered for freshmen scholarships if you apply for admission soon. title: Real Investments, Hands-On Learning Highlight Student Management Fund
text: Real Investments, Hands-On Learning Highlight Student Management Fund - Photo courtesy of Alexander Ziegler Member of the Erin and Kyle Cummings Student Managed Investment Fund (CSMIF). When choosing a college, you’re looking for opportunities to grow - not just academically but through experiences that prepare you for life beyond graduation. One such opportunity at Wichita State University’s Barton School of Business is the Cummings Student Managed Investment Fund (CSMIF) . The fund allows students to manage a $250,000 portfolio, making real-time investment decisions in stocks, bonds and other financial securities. It’s a unique way to take concepts learned in the classroom and apply them in a practical setting, all while working alongside peers from various majors. Even more impactful is the fund’s purpose. The proceeds generated by the investments aren’t kept by the participants - they’re funneled into WSU’s general scholarship fund, helping other students pursue their education. This creates a cycle of support where students directly contribute to the success of their peers. What Draws Students to the Fund? Adam Key, an entrepreneurship major, joined because of his interest in investing and the chance to develop skills for managing his own portfolio. "The opportunity to work with a real fund, invest in real-time, and connect with high-performing Barton School students was a huge draw," Key said. "Being able to network with amazing individuals and learn from hands-on experience has been incredibly rewarding." For students like Key, the fund offers a chance to make decisions with a real impact. He points to the team’s initial investment as a highlight of his experience, particularly the process of determining how much to allocate to cash, stocks and bonds. Watching these decisions translate into real returns has been especially fulfilling. Others, like Michael Goldberg, were drawn by the chance to gain practical experience without the financial risk of using personal money: "I wanted to see how the market affects investments and learn from mistakes in a way that prepares me for future investing," Goldberg said. George Giem, the fund’s president, values the exposure to areas of finance he hadn’t previously considered, like investing in bonds. "It’s easy to lean heavily into stocks as a student, but exploring fixed income investments has been a rewarding experience," Giem said. Beyond the technical aspects, Giem highlights how the fund creates opportunities to meet people and build connections that will last well beyond college. Students chatting outside of the Koch Global Trading Center at Wichita State's Barton School of Business. What Makes the CSMIF Unique at WSU The CSMIF stands out because it’s designed to be accessible and collaborative. Interdisciplinary Participation: Students from all majors can join, whether they’re finance experts or just curious about how investing works. Real-World Application: Guided by an experienced industry advisor, students take on the responsibility of making investment decisions and analyzing market trends. Networking Opportunities: From guest speakers to group projects, students connect with industry professionals and peers with shared interests. What Does Participation Look Like? Fund members meet regularly to discuss the latest developments in financial markets, share insights from their research and collaborate on strategies for future investments. Meetings often feature discussions on current events, hands-on workshops and presentations by guest speakers. These experiences provide practical learning opportunities while fostering teamwork and collaboration. As Key notes, the fund isn’t just for finance majors. "There’s room for students interested in marketing, operations or other aspects of the fund," Key said. "The key is having a passion for learning and a growth-oriented mindset." Why Opportunities Like This Matter Programs like CSMIF reflect Wichita State’s focus on applied learning, where students gain hands-on experience that translates directly into career readiness. Opportunities like this demonstrate the range of possibilities to grow and develop in a collaborative and supportive environment. Whether you’re passionate about investing or looking for ways to expand your knowledge in a team-oriented setting, the CSMIF offers a chance to gain practical experience and make meaningful connections. title: KC Scholar Finds Home Away From Home in the ICT
text: KC Scholar Finds Home Away From Home in the ICT - Photo courtesy of Yuridia Abrego Yuridia Abrego, left, is named a KC Scholar along with her fellow classmates at Ruskin High School in Kansas City, Missouri. Whenever I talk to my friends back home, they always ask me, “Why did you go to the middle of nowhere? All of your friends and family are here, are you sure you want to start all over?” My answer has always been that it is worth it. Wichita State offers many resources I haven’t seen on other campuses. For example, they have partnerships with businesses, such as Spirit AeroSystems and the National Institute for Aviation Research (NIAR) here on campus. That means I can get an internship and maybe even land my future job without even having to drive off campus! Coming from Kansas City, I know that even though you might leave the city, the city never leaves you. Fortunately, Wichita is a pretty big city! It has many places where you can go and hang out with friends. Not to mention the countless restaurants they have here. They have a ton of local businesses waiting for your support. I’m always discovering new restaurants and trying new foods. Even though I miss my friends at home, I have met some amazing people here in Wichita. My friends here have shown me nothing but support, and everything combined made the transition from Kansas City to Wichita seamless. For as long as I can remember, I’ve always known that I didn’t want to stay home for college. I wanted to experience the typical college life, living in a dorm and being able to at least feel as if I was free from my parents. Realistically, I love my family too much and I knew I couldn’t move away too far. That’s why I decided to keep my college options closer than what I originally anticipated. Wichita State is about a three-hour drive from Kansas City, so sometimes I go home on weekends to spend time with my parents and my sisters. A downside of most out-of-state colleges is having to pay an out-of-state tuition fee. Fortunately, Wichita State offered me the Shocker City Partnership Tuition Discount , which allowed me to attend WSU at the in-state tuition rate. With the discount, I felt less burdened by the financial pressures of attending college. However, I didn’t stop there. During my junior and senior years of high school, I applied for scholarships ranging from small $500 awards to full-ride scholarships. I wanted to make sure that I was getting my degree with the least amount of debt. Photo courtesy of Yuridia Abrego Yuridia Abrego, left, decked out in green for the College of Engineering during Clash of the Colleges. Like many Kansas City students, I applied to the $50,000 KC Scholars Traditional Scholarship in my junior year. I remember sitting down in AP Language, typing my essay, while my teacher Ms. Pittard walked by, making sure we were working. I was so determined to win the scholarship that I had not only my English teacher proofread it, but also two of my Upward Bound advisors. After I submitted my application, the worst part came - having to wait until the winners were announced. After several months, I sat in class, oblivious to what was to happen next. My English teacher came and pulled out five of us from class. When we reached the cafeteria, we were announced as the KC Scholars winners for the class of 2024. I couldn’t believe what just happened. My mom was also there, and I remember seeing the proud look on her face and knowing that my hard work paid off. Without KC Scholars, I would not have been able to attend college debt-free. Their scholarship has helped me focus on my other needs instead of my financial needs. Instead of working every spare moment I have in between classes, I can enjoy the fun side of college: hanging out with friends, going to campus events and volunteering in the community. For my future KC Scholar friends, I hope you understand the opportunity you have earned! It is not just a scholarship; it’s a family that supports you throughout college to make sure you graduate. Take advantage of the resources that KC Scholars and Wichita State offer you. Both made it possible for me to even attend college, and that’s why I am proud to be a Shocker! title: School Counseling Program Leverages Resources To Support Student Learning
text: School Counseling Program Leverages Resources To Support Student Learning - Photo courtesy of Lyndsey Brown The School Counseling program at Wichita State is committed to more than just academic preparation— it's about cultivating confident, connected and competent school counselors who are ready to lead and serve in their communities. One of the most impactful ways the program supports this mission is through intentional networking and professional development opportunities that enrich student learning and elevate their training experience. Equipping Students with Real-World Tools Through a grant, WSU’s School Counseling program created a School Counseling Resource Closet , a unique lending library stocked with curriculum kits, therapeutic games, books and classroom tools. Practicum and internship students can check out these materials to try out evidence-based interventions and activities at their field sites. This hands-on access empowers students to experiment, reflect, and grow in their professional practice—all while building confidence and competence in real-world settings. Elevating Access to National and State Conferences Professional development can be cost-prohibitive, especially for graduate students. That’s why Wichita State has prioritized grant-funded conference attendance to ensure its students have access to learning opportunities beyond the classroom. Students have traveled to the American School Counselor Association (ASCA) Conference and the Kansas School Counselor Association (KSCA) Conference, gaining exposure to the latest research, best practices and national conversations shaping the future of school counseling. These experiences not only deepen content knowledge but also strengthen students’ sense of identity within the broader professional community. Fostering Leadership from Day One Wichita State students aren’t just attending conferences—they’re taking the stage. The program actively connects students to leadership positions within the KSCA board, encouraging early engagement in advocacy, governance and strategic planning for the profession. These opportunities give students a voice and a seat at the table, nurturing a new generation of school counseling leaders who understand the value of service and collaboration. Bringing Experts to Campus To further bridge the gap between theory and practice, the program frequently invites nationally recognized school counseling leaders to engage with students. Whether through keynote sessions at the on-campus KSCA Conference or through in-class panels and knowledge shares, students learn directly from changemakers in the field. These interactions foster meaningful dialogue, spark inspiration and help students see themselves as contributors to the evolving narrative of school counseling. Building SEL Capacity Across Kansas In summer 2025, the program will host an SEL Camp for educators across the state—a space where teachers, counselors, and school leaders can deepen their understanding of social-emotional learning and explore how to better integrate it into their school communities. From classroom to conference halls, Wichita State University’s School Counseling program is redefining what it means to prepare school counselors. By investing in professional development, leadership cultivation, and real-world application, the program is not only enriching student learning—it’s shaping the future of school counseling in Kansas and beyond. The School Counseling Program is a graduate program and accepts students with a bachelor's degree from any area of study. More about WSU's School Counseling Program Blog home All posts Dr. Lyndsey Brown Dr. Lyndsey Brown is an Assistant Clinical Professor in the Department of Intervention Services & Leadership in Education at Wichita State University, where she also coordinates the School Counseling program. Since joining WSU in 2022, she has continued her dedication to advancing the school counseling profession. Named the 2021 Kansas School Counselor of the Year, Dr. Brown is passionate about supporting counselors across the state as they develop comprehensive programs that promote student success. title: Students Create Stunning Costumes for Kids With Disabilities Through Non-Profit
text: Students Create Stunning Costumes for Kids With Disabilities Through Non-Profit - Photo courtesy of Maya Douglas The WSU chapter of Walkin' & Rollin' Costumes with their Fall 2023 project for Miranda - a Moana-themed costume. Walkin’ & Rollin’ Costumes is an organization that builds costumes for kids who use wheelchairs or walkers. title: Humans of Wichita State - Karina
text: Humans of Wichita State - Karina - Photo by Matt Crow/Undergraduate Admissions Why did I choose to transfer to Wichita State? What was the transfer process like, and what tips would I give to others starting it? Transferring to WSU was a smooth transition. When I started the process, I reached out to a pre-professional health advisor. As a pre-dental student, I had a lot of questions about my degree options. Meeting with an advisor helped me choose the right classes, stay on track with dental school prerequisites and keep up with deadlines. I highly recommend that any student considering transferring speak with an advisor or admissions representative at WSU, they help make the process easier. How did my credits transfer, and what tools helped me along the way? title: What is Accreditation and Why Does It Matter?
text: What is Accreditation and Why Does It Matter? - Wichita State Strategic Communications Part of the college decision making process is researching different institutions and the programs they offer. One important – often overlooked – part of that is knowing if your school and/or degree program is accredited. What is Accreditation? Accreditation is a quality assurance process that higher education institutions undergo to ensure their academic programs meet established standards of excellence. In the U.S., this process is overseen by recognized accrediting agencies and monitored by the Department of Education. There are two types: Institutional accreditation - evaluates the entire university Programmatic (or specialty) accreditation - focuses on specific departments or programs Why Does It Matter? Accreditation affects nearly every part of your college experience: Financial Aid - Only students at accredited institutions are eligible for federal financial aid under Title IV of the Higher Education Act (HEA) of 1965. Transfer Credits - Accredited schools are more likely to accept credits from other accredited institutions. Graduate School and Employment - Some graduate programs and employers may require degrees from accredited programs. Licensure and Certification - Some careers (such as nursing or teaching) may require graduation from an accredited program to sit for licensing exams. Wichita State’s Accreditation Wichita State University has been regionally accredited by the Higher Learning Commission since 1927. In addition, many of Wichita State’s academic programs hold specialized accreditation. The full breakdown of accredited programs is reported by the Office of Assessment & Accreditation . So next time you're researching a school or talking with an admissions representative, make sure to check the university's accreditation! title: How Do You Pick a Major?
text: How Do You Pick a Major? - Photo courtesy of Lin Lindstrom Lin Lindstrom at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science. Photo courtesy of Lin Lindstrom Lin Lindstrom at the Georgia Aquarium. In third grade, the question “What am I going to be when I grow up?” felt so easy. You just said, “I want to be a fireman!” or “I want to be an astronaut,” or in my case, “I want to be a stay-at-home mom!” But now, as you enter college—and with the current economic climate making it much harder to stay home with the kids—you’re forced to revisit that question: What do I want to be when I grow up? Picking a major is possibly the most daunting task as an incoming college student. Each major has so many intricacies, requirements and classes, with all different focuses and topics. It's hard to decide what to study, and it is even harder to decide what to do with that degree. But, for now, let's tackle the first question: how do you decide on a major? The first step to deciding what you want for your major is to look inward. While it may sound cheesy, you are your own best friend. You know yourself better than anyone else in this world. So, as you are picking your degree plan, discuss these questions with yourself. What Interests You? What makes you want to learn more? Was there a particular subject in school that you loved to learn more about? A specific topic you liked to research? And if not in school, what posts do you see online that draw you in? What makes you want to know more? These are the types of questions to think about when discovering what your interests are. For me, it was sharks! I loved to see posts of sharks online, both the informational and silly ones. After learning more and more about sharks and marine science through apps like Instagram and TikTok, I began to read books and take more classes on environmental and marine biology. Now I plan on devoting my future to becoming a shark biologist. These interests don’t have to be rooted in your education, they can come from anywhere! What Are Your Hobbies? How do you spend your free time? Do you prefer indulging in the arts or physical activity? Do you like to spend time with friends, or do you prefer to be alone? Do you like working with kids? These questions will help guide you in picking what major will be the most fulfilling for you. You want your major to be something you enjoy doing. If there is no passion in the degree path you pick, finishing the degree will be much harder. And the biggest thing is make sure you are picking a major that YOU want, not one your friends or family might have chosen for you. These people want the best for you, but they are not you. College is your time to begin discovering who you are and what you want to do. So, if you like painting more than engineering, don’t feel pressured to choose the one that isn’t true to you. Photo courtesy of Lin Lindstrom Lin Lindstrom, center, with a shark at the Georgia Aquarium. What Does Future You Look Like? Now going back to that age-old question - What do you want to be when you grow up? Consider what career field you want to go into. Do you want to be in healthcare or research? Do you want to be a doctor, dentist, biologist, teacher, politician, engineer, sculptor, etc. And if you do not have a specific career in mind, consider what you want to do more of in the future. Do you want to devote your time to helping people? Do you want to become engaged in politics? Do you want to start your own business? These questions can help build a foundation for what you want your future to be, and help you find a degree path to get you there. Even if you have no idea what you want for your future, that is ok too! College is a time for exploration, and you will find many career paths you had no idea existed. At Wichita State for instance, the Shocker Career Accelerator (SCA) often hosts career fairs for students looking for new job opportunities. If you are looking to discover some of these programs and businesses, feel free to stop by! Getting connected with SCA also provides support in your college journey. Through their PathwayU program, they guide you through a personalized career exploration process to see what degree and career fits you best. If you are undecided, do not feel like you need to rush into finding a major or degree plan. Wichita State offers several opportunities to students who are undecided on a major to discover what major is best for them. As a first-year student coming in, you are welcome to start as an undecided student. Throughout your first year as undecided, you can take many different classes to discover what degree path may be the best for you. If you struggle on deciding just one program, we also have other degree paths for just that! Our Fairmount College of Liberal Arts and Sciences offers a General Studies major where you can choose one main area of study through LAS, and two additional areas from any other department or college. The Cohen Honors College also offers Honors Baccalaureate . In this program, you can choose two to three concentrations from at least two academic colleges and create your own plan of study. Not deciding a major does not mean you are falling behind, it means you have so many more opportunities to explore! Now that you are all grown up and headed off to college, you are likely beginning to realize that the “What do you want to be when you grow up?” presentation wasn’t actually as simple as your third-grade teacher made it seem. There are so many different possibilities, careers and studies out there for you to choose from, and it can be a lot of pressure. Just know, you are not alone. No matter where you go or what you do, you will always have people in your corner to support you and help guide you along the right path. You don’t need to decide your future now, you have a whole life ahead of you. And who knows, maybe someday you could live your childhood dream of being a stay-at-home mom! title: Shocker Engineering Academy: A Jumpstart for New Students
text: Shocker Engineering Academy: A Jumpstart for New Students - Photo courtesy of Jamil West Attendees of Shocker Engineering Academy (SEA). Shocker Engineering Academy (SEA) is the week before classes start in the fall. It’s made for incoming first generation college students studying engineering. Not only does it help you get acquainted with campus resources like the Shocker Career Accelerator , CARE Team and GEEKS Tutoring (tutoring center for engineering) but it is jumpstarts your connection to the college community . I did SEA before my freshman year and had no idea what to expect. The first day was all about group bonding. We went to a YMCA camp and essentially hung out all day. We went canoeing, climbed a rock tower, did archery and had the opportunity to go on this huge rope swing (yikes). I met some awesome people that I still talk to now two years later. The rest of the week includes sessions that get you acquainted with the resources I mentioned above as well as some much-appreciated math review to get you ready for class. In between the information sessions, you also get to build a GoBabyGo car (by far my favorite part). GoBabyGo is a club on campus that modifies off-the-shelf ride-on toy cars for kids with disabilities. Building a car teaches you engineering foundations like wiring a simple circuit and basic design principles, as well as how to work in a team. Photo courtesy of Jamil West GoBabyGo at Shocker Engineering Academy (SEA). The second highlight of the week was the big spoons tournament we had. The mentors create a bracket and trophies. There’s also a loser’s game where we play for the biggest loser (gets their own special trophy), and the winner gets their shot at redemption and plays in the finals. Many of the mentors (like me), are also part of other clubs like National Society of Black Engineers and Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers , so they can get you plugged in to groups like those. SEA is a great way to jumpstart your college career and is an all-around fun week. I can’t recommend it enough. title: “Student Centered. Innovation Driven.®” – More Than Just a Motto
text: “Student Centered. Innovation Driven.®” – More Than Just a Motto - Photo by Matt Crow/Undergraduate Admissions Students inside the Shocker Success Center near the "Student Centered. Innovation Driven" banner. Wichita State brands itself as “Student Centered. Innovation Driven.®” But what does that mean, exactly? Student-centeredness is not new to higher education. A quick online search will yield broad definitions for the concept, and one institution’s practice might not match other's At Wichita State, student-centeredness is a commitment to holistic student success through a wide range of opportunities and resources offered to Shockers. Access and Affordability Before a student even begins their college journey, they have the advantage of lower costs and fewer roadblocks. Wichita State is proud to be Kansas’ most affordable research university , as well as a more affordable option compared to many regional research institutions. This means students pay less tuition over their academic career. On top of that, Wichita State is an access-oriented university that doesn’t hang its hat on selectivity, nor does it take pleasure in denying students in the name of prestige. With a more than 90 percent acceptance rate, Wichita State is focused more on celebrating all students who choose to become Shockers and helping them reach their academic and professional goals. Success Resources One way to promote student-centeredness – put student support systems right in the middle of campus. The Shocker Success Center houses dozens of departments solely focused on providing students the resources they need. From academic assistance such as tutoring and supplemental instruction, to support for international, military & veteran and TRIO students, the Success Center is the place to go! Career Focus With a heavy emphasis on applied learning, Wichita State is not satisfied with only getting students their degree, but also ensuring they have a clear career path upon graduation. The development of the Innovation Campus has brought numerous business and industry partners within walking distance of students’ doorsteps. Not only that but growing local and regional partnerships with the university has opened the doors to continued applied learning opportunities for students of all majors. At the heart of positive student outcomes is the Shocker Career Accelerator (SCA) . Students have year-round access to the SCA’s professionals who assist with career exploration, interview prep, resume building, free professional photos and LinkedIn optimization just to name a few. SCA also engages with hundreds of employers and hosts several on-campus career fairs throughout the year allowing students networking opportunities. Student-centeredness can mean many things. At Wichita State, it means the roadblocks to getting started are few and there are plenty of people and resources along the way to ensure students see the fruits of their labor. title: Earning Credit in Picturesque France - Sophie's Study Abroad Story
text: Earning Credit in Picturesque France - Sophie's Study Abroad Story - Photo courtesy of Sophie Walter Sophie Walter with the summer study abroad group in Biarritz, France - a seaside town on the Basque coast. Photo courtesy of Sophie Walter Sophie Walter, left, and members of her study abroad group pose for a photo in front of hydrangeas in Pau, France. Ever since middle school, I dreamed of studying abroad. So when it came time to choose a college, I made sure to find a school with strong opportunities to study internationally. Wichita State University checked that box. WSU has an amazing study abroad program, offering experiences not only across the globe , but also within the United States . One of the biggest perks: students pay their tuition and fees at Wichita State rates, making it financially accessible. Photo courtesy of Sophie Walter Sophie Walter, center, with members of the study abroad group on a gondola in Pau, France. This past summer, I had the privilege of joining the Barton School of Business on a study abroad trip to Pau, France. Along with about 14 other business students and two incredible faculty members, Dorothy Harpool and Seth Crockwell, I spent several weeks immersed in French culture while completing coursework. Our schedule was just what we needed - classes ran Monday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., which meant long weekends to explore. The courses counted toward our entrepreneurial experience and international business requirements - two classes every business major needs. It was incredible how I got to take required classes while being abroad. Financially, I was extremely grateful to receive the Bassi Family Scholarship, a $5,000 award specifically for business students studying abroad. That support made this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity possible for me. Photo courtesy of Sophie Walter Sophie Walter and Ellie Stringer inside of the Louvre in Paris, France. Before the program officially began, a few friends and I spent three days in Paris. We explored the Eiffel Tower, cruised along the Seine River, visited the Louvre, got to see Notre Dame, and wandered the streets of the city. During the program, one of the highlights was a group trip to Biarritz, a stunning coastal town located on the border between France and Spain. We toured the city, learned about its history, and then my friends and I decided to stay the weekend. Those few days were unforgettable—swimming in the Atlantic Ocean, exploring the farmers' market, attending a music festival, and indulging in some of the best food I’ve ever had. The program brought together students who started as classmates but quickly became friends. Living, learning, and exploring a new country together gave us a unique bond that’s hard to put into words. From late-night conversations to spontaneous adventures, we shared experiences that no one else will ever quite understand. If you’ve ever thought about studying abroad, my advice is simple: go for it. It’s not just about where you’ll go - it’s about who you’ll become along the way. title: Transforming Education
text: Transforming Education - Graphic by Joey Fonkert/Undergraduate Admissions I’ve been affiliated with Wichita State for more than 25 years and even I get chills when I think about how far our university has come in that time. While enrollment typically hovered around 14,500 students annually for much of the last few decades, it’s eyebrow-raising that we just announced fall 2025 enrollment above 18,000 Shockers for the first time ever in in the university’s 130-year history. For an institution that started with just 16 students back in 1895, we’ve created sustained enrollment momentum in a time when students and families are pondering deeply about the return on investment for college. Here’s a few highlights from our fall 2025 enrollment data: Wichita State achieved the highest headcount (18,458) and credit hours (170,521) in the university’s history. For the fifth year in a row , the freshmen class was larger than 1,600 students. The five largest freshmen classes in the university’s history have all occurred since 2021. Transfer students are continually choosing Shocker Nation, with the university being the state’s top transfer destination for 14 years in a row . Data indicates students from both two-year colleges and four-year universities in Kansas are transferring to Wichita State at a higher volume than any other school in the state. Gap-year students who enter Wichita State after taking time away from education post-high school have more than doubled since 2021. Since 2015, the number of new students living on campus has increased by 45 percent . Expansion of Wichita State's concurrent and dual enrollment programs led to more than 1,600 students gaining early access to college credit. Transforming Education It’s no coincidence we’re hitting our all-time stride at a time when higher education is reflecting on what it needs to be for the future. It’s been a series of big bets that have paid off, fueling enrollment growth. Here’s a look at the transformational jumps Wichita State has made to get us to this point. More than 10 years ago now, Wichita State made a big bet on our now iconic 120-acre Innovation Campus . Closing an 18-hole golf course on campus yielded some upset community golfers, but the big payoff has been more than 20 new facilities , including two new residence halls, a new on-campus YMCA, restaurants and retail options and strategically potent partnerships with companies and organizations that hire our students for internships, research and applied learning opportunities. Our focus on applied learning is what separates Wichita State from all the rest. Each year our students earn more than $30 million in applied learning opportunities and internships spread across more than 9,000 experiences our students annually take advantage of. Our students not only graduate with the required courses, but they typically have multiple internships that demonstrate how they applied what they’ve learned with employers and community partners - such as Lauren, a student from Oklahoma, who shares how she was propelled by Wichita State to reach for the stars through an internship at NASA. Wichita State made an investment in student success in the last several years, resulting in a persistence rate increase for the fourth year in a row and an overall six percent increase since 2021. One of the biggest drivers for this is the $17 million investment in the new Shocker Success Center , which has created a home for student success and support-oriented offices all in one place. Our next big bet is coming fast. In spring 2027, we’re scheduled to open the new Wichita Biomedical Campus downtown, a partnership between Wichita State and the University of Kansas. We’ll bring together Wichita State’s Health Professions programs, such as nursing, physical therapy, physician associate and more with KU’s medical and pharmacy schools, which were already located in our city. This partnership will command nearly a half-a-million square feet downtown, eventually enroll more than 3,000 students and reflect an investment of more than $300 million in Wichita’s downtown . Most importantly, though, a shared clinical space will allow our two universities plus WSU Tech to train our students together. When we train our healthcare practitioners with one another, we know we’ll have improved patient outcomes and better-prepared professionals. Cracking the Code for Future Generations I have the great fortune to be a part of the Wichita community through serving on boards and being involved in events all over our city. This allows me the opportunity to engage with people on a regular basis, hearing what their unfiltered opinions are of our university these days. I can confirm Wichita State students, supporters and alumni walk around with a bit more swagger these days and I’d note wearing black and yellow has never been more popular (with all due respect to our Shocker Men’s Basketball Final Four run in 2013). While we welcome all seniors and transfers to apply now , we know you may still need a bit more fuel to fire your interest in Wichita State. One way to do just that is by viewing our episode on Amazon Prime TV’s streaming series, The College Tour , which was just released this summer. As the first and only university in Kansas to be featured, you can access more than an hour of highly visual, in-depth content that showcases many facets of Shocker life, all through digestible two-minute clips of what our university offers to today’s modern students. It’s not hyperbole to say Wichita State has cracked the code on one way to be a university that is leaning into the future of what families expect from an institution of higher education, and what employers and communities need from both our graduates and the university itself. If ever there was a time to join Shocker Nation, this is the moment where you can be a part of a university that is rising above the trend line of higher education. title: Things To Know When Filling Out the 2025–26 FAFSA Form
text: Things To Know When Filling Out the 2025–26 FAFSA Form - Photo by Matt Crow/Undergraduate Admissions FAFSA season is here – let’s get you ready! College is a big investment, but financial aid can make it affordable. The 2026-2027 FAFSA is now open and it’s the key to unlock grants, scholarships, work-study and federal loans. Completing the FAFSA early gives you the best chance at receiving the most support and for us to provide you with an offer to help you compare college costs. For Wichita State University, the 2026-2027 FAFSA covers the fall 2026, spring 2027 and summer 2027 semesters. Key Dates to Know: FAFSA Opened: Oct. 1, 2025 Wichita State Priority Date: Dec. 1, 2025 Final Date to Submit: June 30, 2026 Steps to Complete Your FAFSA: Create your studentaid.gov account (FSA ID) Gather your documents: Social Security Number /Alien Registration Number 2024 federal tax info Records of child support, untaxed income and current bank balances Log in to studentaid.gov and start your FAFSA List up to 20 colleges, including Wichita State. Our Code is 001950 Sign and submit Need help figuring out who needs to contribute info (like a parent or spouse)? Use the FAFSA Parent Wizard . If you experience any issues while attempting to complete your application, you can access Federal Student Aid’s Help Center 24/7/365. You can call at 1-800-433-3243, live chat with Aiden the Owl or send an email through their online form. What Happens After You Submit the FAFSA? Once you hit “submit” on your FAFSA, here’s what to expect next: Confirmation Email You’ll receive a confirmation from Federal Student Aid. Keep this for your records — it means your application was successfully submitted. FAFSA Processing Your FAFSA will be processed by the U.S. Department of Education. This usually takes a few days, but can take longer during peak times. Student Aid Report (SAR) You’ll get a Student Aid Report summarizing the information you submitted. As a Wichita-native, I chose Wichita State University for its affordability and scholarship opportunities, convenient location and community-based campus. The ability to stay at home with family, work, earn my degree and still be a part of the many clubs and organizations at Wichita State solidified my choice. If you graduated from a non-accredited high school or were homeschooled, you must: Achieve an ACT of 21 or higher OR a minimum combined SAT ERW+M score of at least 1060, AND have a cumulative 2.25 or higher GPA on a 4.00 scale. If you enroll in college courses while in high school, you must also achieve a 2.00 GPA or higher in those courses. If you obtained your GED, you must: For GED tests from 2014 and on: Have a minimum score of 150 on each sub test and an overall score of 680 to be admitted. For GED tests from 2002-2013: Have a minimum score of 510 on each sub test and an overall score of 2550 to be admitted.
